text:
The coffee in David Vance’s chipped mug vibrated with a low, almost imperceptible hum. It wasn’t the fridge, nor the old floorboards groaning under the weight of the decaying Blackwood Bay Lodge. This vibration seemed to resonate from beneath the very foundation, a frequency just at the edge of hearing that set his teeth on edge. He traced the lines of a local police report with a skeptical finger, the ink blurring slightly with the tremor.

The report detailed a minor incident at the old cannery — not theft, not even a break-in, but a peculiar act of destruction. Someone had taken a fishing net, meticulously woven and hung to dry, and sliced it into precise, ragged strips, as if with a sudden, violent urge to dismantle. No motive, no suspects. Just the act itself, a senseless fracturing of order. It echoed a recent whisper he’d caught at the diner, about old Man Hemlock, quiet for fifty years, suddenly bellowing at the sky over a split fence post.

Blackwood Bay had always hummed with its own peculiar rhythm, but lately, that hum felt like a fracture, like the world itself was pulling apart at the seams. Outside, the fog that clung to the bay seemed thicker, churning against the docks with an agitated current that felt less like tide and more like a restless, unseen heart beating just beneath the surface.
